author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: A Refugee at the Yard
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass two
content:
The stranger at the workshop door wore an old Commonwealth coat with the insignia torn from the shoulder.

That was the first thing Danse noticed.

The second was the way they kept one hand near their satchel, as though someone had taught them to expect their belongings to be searched.

"Are you taking repair work?" the stranger asked.

Danse glanced at the bent metal housing they were carrying.

"Depending on the damage."

They set it carefully on the counter.

It was a pump regulator, patched twice, with a burn mark along one side.

"Can you fix it?"

"I can assess it."

The stranger looked over Danse's shoulder at me.

"Does he run this place?"

Danse went very still.

I understood the question before he did.

"We share the work," I answered. "And we don't ask people to join a faction before we'll look at their equipment."

They exhaled.

"Good."

Their name was Ash. They had come through the Brasswatch Door with permission from a local courier, following a rumor that the workshop repaired things without demanding military loyalty. They wanted a regulator fixed, temporary shelter, and a job that did not require them to tell strangers what they were.

Danse examined the housing.

"This part isn't the original."

"No."

"Where did you get the replacement?"

"A machine shop near Bunker Hill."

"That's a dangerous route."

Ash's jaw tightened.

"I know."

He looked at their face again and seemed to hear how his question had landed.

"Can I open the casing?" he asked.

Ash nodded.

That was a better question.

We took the regulator apart on a clean mat. The internal coil had been repaired with copper wire too thin for the load, and the contacts were worn almost through. Danse explained the problem without blaming the person who had made the last repair.

Ash listened carefully.

"You can fix it?"

"Yes. It will take a day."

"I can pay with work."

"What kind?"

"Woodworking. Cleaning. Inventory. I learn quickly."

"Do you have references?"

Ash's expression changed.

Danse saw it.

"That was a standard question," he said.

"In the Commonwealth, standard questions get people killed," Ash replied.

The room went quiet.

Outside, the temporary water station creaked as someone filled a jug. Pip called a greeting to a neighbor. The world sounded entirely ordinary, which made the fear in Ash's voice harder to ignore.

"I didn't mean to interrogate you," Danse said.

Ash looked at him.

"You sound like the Brotherhood."

He did not deny it.

"I was Brotherhood."

"I know."

The two words changed the room.

Danse's hands stopped moving over the regulator. For a moment, I could see him reaching for the authority he once understood. Then he put both hands flat on the table.

"What do you need from us right now?" he asked.

Ash blinked.

"A place to stay tonight. A door that locks. No one asking me for a serial number."

Danse looked at me.

"We have a spare room behind the yard," I said. "But Neri handles temporary housing. We can ask what is available, privately."

Ash nodded.

"Will you tell anyone why I came?"

"Only what you give us permission to tell," I said.

They looked at Danse.

He took a breath.

"I won't report you."

Ash's face did not soften.

"That's a promise people make when they want something."

Danse accepted the criticism without argument.

"Then judge me by what I do."

We spent the afternoon working quietly.

Ash proved good with wood. They fixed the crooked shelf that had irritated everyone for a week. Tamsin stopped by and approved the repair with a nod. Pip brought bread and water and did not ask questions.

Danse kept his distance unless Ash needed an instruction. At one point, he caught himself saying "You will" and stopped.

"Would you be willing to check the left bracket?" he asked instead.

Ash's mouth twitched.

"Sure."

Later, when Ash went to speak with Neri, Danse sat on the back steps with the old regulator in his hands.

"You knew," I said.

"Suspected."

"About Ash?"

"Yes."

He looked at the torn insignia on the coat hanging by the workbench.

"I used to believe every synth was a threat. That there was no meaningful difference between identity and manufacture."

"And now?"

"Now I know what it feels like to have someone decide what I am before I speak."

I sat beside him.

"That doesn't automatically make you safe for everyone who's been hurt by that belief."

"No."

He said it without flinching.

"I don't want Ash to forgive me," he continued. "I want to make sure the repair is sound and that nobody uses this place to hunt them."

"That's a good place to start."

He looked at me.

"You don't have to reassure me."

"I wasn't going to."

He gave a short, surprised laugh.

That evening, Neri arranged a private room for Ash near the square. The key belonged to Ash; nobody else would enter without asking. The housing register listed only the help Ash had consented to request.

The next day, we finished the regulator.

Danse explained what he'd replaced and showed Ash how to inspect the contacts without dismantling the whole housing. Ash followed every step.

"Does it work?" they asked.

"Under the tested load, yes. You'll need a new coil eventually."

"Then I'll come back if I need one."

"You can."

They looked up at him.

"Is that an invitation or an order?"

Danse paused.

"An invitation."

Ash nodded.

They paid with two hours of shelf repairs and left through the Brasswatch Door after choosing a safe return time.

No one applauded. No one announced that a former Paladin had become a better man. A stranger had received a repair without surrendering their private history.

That was enough.

When the workshop closed, I found Danse cleaning the tools.

"You've been quiet," I said.

"Thinking."

"Dangerous."

He set the wrench down.

"Do you ever wonder whether the people we've hurt would prefer we stayed away from them?"

"Yes."

"Sometimes I think the best I can do is leave them alone."

"Sometimes that is the best thing."

He looked at me.

"And the other times?"

"Ask what they need. Believe the answer. Do the work."

Danse was silent for a while.

Then he reached for my hand.

"Will you stay for dinner?"

"I'd like that."

He smiled, almost shy.

We went home without carrying the day's good deed like a medal. I liked him better for it.

The next morning, the repaired shelf was still straight.

There was no lesson written on it.

It simply held what people needed it to hold.
